reasons: The finding is correctly classified: Section 11.1 commits Corio to a five-year initial term with automatic renewals, and the only exits in Section 11.2 are material breach and insolvency, so there is no customer termination-for-convenience right in a multi-year term — walk-away territory under T4C and a clear failure of the fallback (60–90 days' notice with capped fee).

The redline is directionally correct and minimal: it inserts a standalone customer convenience right on 30 days' written notice with a pro-rata refund of prepaid fees and no termination fee, tracking the model language, and leaves the existing term and breach-termination provisions intact.

The failed deterministic check ('Customer convenience termination present') is a phrasing artifact — the inserted text names the customer by its party name ('Corio may terminate ... for convenience upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice'), which the alias regex did not capture; substantively the required right is present.
The comment is accurate, concise, in the required voice, explains the five-year lock-in rationale, and offers the 60-day fallback.

Minor, non-fatal: the inserted paragraph is unnumbered while the rationale calls it 'new 11.2' (an existing 11.2 already exists); it should be numbered 11.3 or the section renumbered on execution. The decision not to redline the mutual 30-day non-renewal notice is defensible since it is an end-of-term, symmetric right that also preserves our own exit flexibility, and it is disclosed in the rationale.
